title: Akwamu: The Kingdom That Kept the Castle Keys

pages.text: Cross the Adomi Bridge over the River Volta and turn towards the quiet town of Akwamufie. In the palace there, the chiefs keep a bunch of heavy iron keys. They do not open any door in the town. They are the keys of Christiansborg Castle at Osu in Accra, about a hundred kilometres away by road, a castle built by Europeans and later used as the seat of Ghana’s government. How did the keys of a castle by the sea come to rest in a small town beside the Volta? The answer is one of the boldest stories in our history.

pages.text: Akwamu was an Akan state. In the early 1600s its capital, Nyanoase, stood in the hills near present-day Nsawam. The position was well chosen. The paths that carried gold from the forest down to the forts on the coast passed through Akwamu country, and the kingdom grew rich by taxing the traders who used them. With that wealth, its kings bought guns and built an army that fought in organised wings: front, left, right, and rear. Other Akan states later copied this plan, and it shaped the way chiefs are ranked to this day.

pages.text: Under King Ansa Sasraku, Akwamu turned towards the sea. Between 1677 and 1681, its army conquered the Ga kingdom and took control of Accra and its trade. More victories followed. By the early 1700s, Akwamu ruled a strip of coast about 400 kilometres long, from near Winneba in the west, across the Volta, to Ouidah in present-day Benin. A young prince from the forest spent part of his youth at the Akwamu court and watched how the state was run. His name was Osei Tutu, and he would go on to found the Asante kingdom.

pages.text: In 1693, an Akwamu trader named Asameni carried out a daring plan. He was well known to the Danes in Christiansborg Castle, because he often did business with them. One day he arrived with about eighty men, saying that they wished to buy guns. The Danes let them in. The visitors had hidden powder and shot in their clothes. They loaded the guns they were shown, turned them on the soldiers, and took the castle. Asameni raised his own flag, called himself governor, and traded with passing ships for a whole year.

pages.text: In 1694, the Danes paid a large sum in gold to get their castle back. Akwamu returned the building, but the keys were kept, and they have stayed with the Akwamu ever since. Power, however, makes enemies. Akwamu’s rule was harsh, and its neighbours suffered from its raids. In 1730, the Akyem and their allies joined forces and broke the kingdom. The royal family and many of the people crossed the Volta and built a new capital at Akwamufie, where their descendants live today. The empire had lasted about fifty years.

pages.text: Akwamu was small, yet it left large marks. Its way of arranging an army was adopted by Asante. It showed that an African state could bargain with Europeans as an equal, and even outwit them. Its fall carries a warning as well: a state that rules by fear alone will find that its neighbours unite against it. The keys at Akwamufie are a reminder of all this. Kings, castles, and governments come and go. What lasts is how a people is remembered, and whether its neighbours speak of it with respect or with relief.

activities.question: How did Akwamu first become rich?
options: By taxing traders on the paths between the forest and the coast

activities.question: How did Asameni and his men capture Christiansborg Castle?
options: They dug a tunnel under the walls
They entered as customers and turned the guns on the soldiers

activities.question: Why did Akwamu fall in 1730?
options: Its neighbours, who had suffered under its rule, united against it

activities.question: Apply it: A class prefect gets his way only by threatening others. Using the lesson of Akwamu, what is likely to happen in time?
options: The others will join together against him
He will be made head teacher

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from earliest to latest.
items: Akwamu grows rich at Nyanoase by taxing trade
Akwamu conquers the Ga kingdom and controls Accra
The Danes buy the castle back, but the keys are kept
Akyem and its allies defeat Akwamu, and the people move to Akwamufie
